topics.title: Introduction & Historical Background of Contract Law
explain: Before 1872, Hindu Law and Mohammedan Law governed contracts based on custom and religious texts.
British Presidency Towns applied English Law under the Charter of 1726 based on personal laws or justice and equity.
The Indian Contract Act, 1872 was enacted on April 25, 1872, and came into force on September 1, 1872.
The Act extends to the whole of India following the removal of Article 370.
General principles of contract law are in Sections 1 to 75, while special contracts are in Sections 124 to 238.

flow.title: Evolution of Contract Law in India

topics.example: Before 1872, disputes in presidency towns were decided using the personal religion of the defendant.
mistakes: Confusing the enactment date (25 April 1872) with the enforcement date (1 September 1872).

quiz.q: When did the Indian Contract Act, 1872 come into force?
quiz.why: The Act was enacted on April 25, 1872, but came into force on September 1, 1872.

quiz.q: Which Arabic terms were used for proposal and acceptance under Mohammedan Law?
quiz.why: Under Islamic law, 'Ijab' represented proposal and 'Qabul' represented acceptance.

topics.title: What is a Contract?
explain: Section 2(h) defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law.
A contract requires two elements: an agreement and enforceability by law.
Section 2(e) defines an agreement as every promise forming consideration for each other.
Section 2(b) states that a proposal when accepted becomes a promise.
Social or domestic agreements lack legal enforceability and do not create contracts.

flow.title: Steps to Form a Binding Contract

topics.example: A agrees to sell his car to B for 2 lakh rupees. This creates a legal obligation on both sides.
mistakes: Assuming all agreements are contracts; social agreements are not legally enforceable.

quiz.q: According to Section 2(h) of the Act, a contract is defined as:
quiz.why: Section 2(h) explicitly defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law.

quiz.q: Why could the wife not recover maintenance in Balfour v. Balfour?
o: It was a domestic agreement lacking legal intent
quiz.why: Domestic or social agreements are not intended to create legally binding obligations.

topics.title: Essentials of a Valid Contract
explain: Section 10 requires free consent, competent parties, lawful consideration, and a lawful object.
Agreements must not be expressly declared void under Sections 24 to 30 and 56.
Additional essentials include having two distinct parties and intention to create legal relations.
The agreement must have certainty of meaning and possibility of performance.
Consensus ad idem means both parties agree upon the same thing in the same sense.
topics.example: An agreement to discover treasure by magic cannot be enforced because performance is impossible.
remember: At least two distinct persons are needed; a person cannot contract with himself.
Identity of minds is called consensus ad idem.
mistakes: Believing written registration is required for all contracts; oral contracts are valid unless law specifies otherwise.

quiz.q: Which of the following essentials is directly listed under Section 10?
quiz.why: Free consent is explicitly stated as an essential element inside Section 10.

quiz.q: In State of Gujarat v. Ramanlal S & Co., why was division of firm assets among partners held not to be a sale?
o: Partners are joint owners and cannot be buyer and seller
It was illegal under tax law
quiz.why: A contract requires two separate parties; joint owners cannot sell to themselves.

topics.title: Types of Contracts
explain: By Validity: Valid, Void (Sec 2(j)), Voidable (Sec 2(i)), Illegal, and Unenforceable contracts.
A void contract ceases to be enforceable, while a voidable contract is avoidable by the aggrieved party.
By Formation: Express (words), Implied (conduct), Quasi-contract (law-imposed), and E-contracts.
By Performance: Executed (both performed) and Executory (pending performance).
Executory contracts can be Unilateral (one side pending) or Bilateral (both sides pending).
topics.example: Withdrawing cash from an ATM is a tacit or implied contract created by conduct.
remember: Void ab initio means void from the very beginning.
Agreements collateral to illegal agreements are always void.
mistakes: Confusing void and illegal contracts; all illegal agreements are void, but not all void agreements are illegal.

quiz.q: An agreement enforceable at the option of one party but not at the option of the other is a:
quiz.why: Section 2(i) defines a voidable contract as enforceable at the option of the aggrieved party.

quiz.q: Contracts formed purely by conduct, such as withdrawing cash from an ATM, are called:
quiz.why: Tacit or implied contracts are inferred directly from the conduct of the parties.

topics.title: Proposal or Offer and Its Essentials
explain: Section 2(a) defines an offer as signifying willingness to do or abstain with a view to obtaining assent.
An offer must be made with the intention to create legal relations.
The terms of the offer must be certain, definite, and unambiguous.
An offer must be communicated to the offeree to be complete.
Offers can be General, Specific, Cross, Counter, or Standing/Open offers.

flow.title: Elements of a Valid Offer
steps: Express Willingness to Do or Abstain

topics.example: If a person finds a missing boy without knowing about a reward offer, he cannot claim the reward.
remember: Acceptance in ignorance of an offer confers no legal right (Lalman Shukla case).
A counter offer terminates the original offer.
mistakes: Thinking cross offers form a binding contract; identical offers crossing in transit create no contract.

quiz.q: Why was Lalman denied the reward in Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt?
o: He found the boy without knowledge of the offer
quiz.why: An offer must be communicated; acting in ignorance of an offer does not constitute acceptance.

quiz.q: What is the legal effect of a counter offer on the original offer?
o: It keeps the original offer open
quiz.why: A counter offer constitutes a rejection and termination of the original offer.

topics.title: Offer vs. Invitation to Offer
explain: An offer expresses final willingness to be bound upon acceptance.
An invitation to offer invites the other party to make an offer and negotiate terms.
Catalogues, price tags, prospectus, and auction notices are invitations to offer.
Quoting the lowest cash price in response to an inquiry is an invitation to offer.
Case reference: Harvey v. Facie confirmed that supplying price info is not an offer.
topics.example: Selecting items in a self-service store and bringing them to the cashier is an offer by the buyer.
remember: Price tags, catalogues, and prospectus are invitations to offer, not offers.
Answering a price query is merely information (Harvey v. Facie).
mistakes: Assuming displaying goods in a shop window obligates the shopkeeper to sell; it is only an invitation to offer.

quiz.q: In Harvey v. Facie, quoting the 'Lowest price for Bumper Hall Pen is £900' was held to be:
o: An invitation to offer / statement of price
quiz.why: Quoting the lowest price is a statement of price and invitation to offer, not a binding offer to sell.

quiz.q: When a shop displays goods with price tags attached, the display is legally classified as:
quiz.why: Displaying goods with price tags invites prospective customers to make an offer to purchase.

topics.title: Acceptance and Its Legal Rules
explain: Section 2(b) defines acceptance as signifying assent to a proposal, creating a promise.
Sir William Anson stated acceptance is to offer what a lighted match is to a train of gunpowder.
Acceptance must be absolute, unqualified, and in the prescribed or usual mode.
Acceptance must be communicated; mere mental assent or silence is not acceptance.
Acceptance must be given within the specified or reasonable time before the offer lapses.
topics.example: An offeror cannot state that silence will be treated as acceptance (Felthouse v. Bindley).
remember: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified.
Silence does not amount to acceptance.
mistakes: Believing uncommunicated mental assent creates a binding contract.

quiz.q: According to Sir William Anson, acceptance is compared to:
quiz.why: Anson stated acceptance is to offer what a lighted match is to a train of gunpowder.

quiz.q: Why was the uncle unable to claim the horse in Felthouse v. Bindley?
o: Silence cannot be prescribed as acceptance
quiz.why: An offeror cannot impose a condition that silence will be treated as acceptance.

topics.title: Communication of Offer, Acceptance, and Special Conditions
explain: Communication of offer is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree.
Communication of acceptance is complete against proposer when posted in transmission.
Communication of acceptance is complete against acceptor when it reaches the proposer.
Instantaneous acceptance (phone, fax, email) is complete when received by the offeror.
Special conditions on tickets bind the user if reasonable notice is provided at or before purchase.
topics.example: Conditions printed on an airline ticket bind the passenger if reasonable notice was available.
remember: Proposer is bound as soon as the acceptance letter is posted.
Acceptor is bound only when the acceptance letter reaches the proposer.
mistakes: Thinking the proposer is bound only when he receives or reads the acceptance letter; posting binds him instantly.

quiz.q: As against the proposer, communication of acceptance is complete when:
o: It is put in course of transmission
quiz.why: Under Section 4, acceptance is complete against the offeror as soon as it is posted/transmitted.

quiz.q: When are special terms printed on a ticket binding on a passenger?
o: If reasonable notice is given at or before purchase
quiz.why: Special conditions bind the acceptor if reasonable notice is provided at or before entering the contract.

topics.title: Revocation of Offer and Acceptance
explain: An offer may be revoked anytime before its acceptance is complete against the proposer.
An acceptance may be revoked anytime before communication reaches the proposer.
Offer revocation modes: Notice, lapse of time, default on condition precedent, death, counter offer.
Death or insanity revokes an offer only if known to the acceptor before acceptance.
In Indian law, acceptance sent by post can be revoked before the letter reaches the offeror.
topics.example: A proposes by letter to sell a house to B. A can revoke the offer before B posts his acceptance letter.
remember: Offer can be revoked before acceptance is posted.
Acceptance can be revoked before the acceptance letter reaches the offeror.
mistakes: Assuming an offer cannot be revoked if a deadline was set; it can be revoked anytime before acceptance unless supported by consideration.

quiz.q: Under Section 5, until when can an offeror revoke his proposal?
o: Until the offeree receives the offer
Before acceptance is complete against proposer
quiz.why: A proposal can be revoked anytime before the communication of acceptance is complete against the proposer.

quiz.q: Which of the following does NOT automatically revoke an offer under Section 6?
o: Death of offeror unknown to offeree
quiz.why: Death or insanity revokes an offer only if the fact comes to the knowledge of the acceptor before acceptance.
